## <u>**STATION**</u> 

**Tobacco Dependence**

# 1. <u>**INSTRUCTIONS FOR PATIENT:**</u>

You have experienced daily cough for about 2 months. You went to an urgent care two weeks ago and got a “Z-Pack” and an inhaler which did not help. They also did a chest x-ray and pulmonary function test and TB skin test. They “didn’t find anything.”  You think worry that your smoking might be causing the cough but you have tried to quit in the past and have not been able to. You are thinking about trying to quit, but you are doubtful about your chances of success.

## 1.1. ***Symptoms***

Daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months.  You have a cough in the morning with a little bit of gray mucous. Aside from the mild cough, <u>***you have no other symptoms***</u>.



## 1.2. ***Other history***

No history of asthma or allergy as a child.

No heartburn or reflux symptoms.

No wheezing.

No sick contacts.

No medications except Benadryl as needed.

No nasal congestion. No fever.

No regular exercise.

Allergies: Rash from Penicillin.

Family History: Your father’s mother (a smoker) had a heart attack at age 60.

Your parents are alive and in their 70s.

Three grandparents are alive in their 90s. One died of lung cancer two years ago (she did not smoke). No history of asthma or allergy in the family.

Social History

You are married with two kids. You are a teacher. You were born in US and never traveled outside US. No illegal drug use. No incarceration.

Smoking History (give details as prompted by the physician)

1. You smoke a pack of cigarettes a day since age 15.  You smoke Salem Lights. You switched from the regular Salem’s 8 years ago. You smoke after meals, with your coffee which you take on the back porch as your morning, afternoon, and evening ritual (while you grade papers), in your car when you drive, and during your lunch and planning period.
2. You have tried to quit a total of four times over the years.   You tried once with the patch (which you wore for two weeks) and once with the gum (you chewed only a few pieces when you had bad cravings). You still had cravings despite the medicines, and you didn’t like the taste of the gum, so you doubt the medicines work. Your longest quit attempt was two weeks.
3. Your spouse does not smoke and doesn’t let you smoke in the house. You can’t smoke at school. You do take a smoking break at lunch time, but you have to go out to your car or to a nearby coffee shop with an outdoor patio to smoke.
4. Your 70 year old father has smoked his whole life without health consequences.  Your grandfather still smokes a pipe at 94 years old.
5. You really enjoy smoking because it helps you relax and to concentrate and keep your weight down.

You should pay attention to the student’s behavior towards you if s/he explains the connection between your cough and the need for you to quit smoking. If they point out the connection between your smoking and your cough, and offer additional support, you are willing to try to quit and accept their offer of calling the quitline and using medications if they explain the fact that your symptoms suggest addiction, and offer you help to overcome the addiction with medications.  You doubt the NRT will work, but if they explain the need to take a high enough dose to eliminate withdrawal symptoms then you are willing to try any combination of medications other than the gum. Set a quit date if they suggest it. If they offer counseling, tell them that you are worried it will not fit with your schedule, but if they give you several alternatives that include the quitline or evening or weekend classes, tell them that you are willing to try counseling. If they get into too much blaming, you can get a little defensive. If they don’t offer you support when they suggest you quit, talk about how cigarettes help relieve your stress, and how you have had difficulty concentrating and headaches when you tried to quit before.

If the doctor gives you treatment recommendations that do not include quitting smoking, wait until the two minute warning or they say that they are done and then ask:

- “My partner thinks my cough is because I smoke, but my family all smoke and none of them cough. Do you think I should try to cut down?

## <u>**STATION 10**</u> 

**TOBACCO DEPENDENCE**

<u>**SCENARIO:**</u>

You are working in a busy primary care clinic and are about to see a 32-year-old who complains of cough for the past two months. She was seen at an urgent care center two weeks ago and again last week. The urgent care physician reported that the evaluation was normal and did not identify another cause of the cough.

A previous course of treatment did not help. The urgent care note advises follow up with the primary care physician.

**Case summary**: The patient is a 65-year old man or woman presenting to the emergency department with a history of neck pain over the last several weeks. The pain has become increasingly worse, and is present all day, every day. The patient has also developed weakness of all four extremities, clumsiness, and had an episode of urinary incontinence. Overall, the symptoms are very concerning to the patient. The patient’s past medical history includes colon cancer, which had been treated with surgical resection two years ago. The patient does not know what stage the cancer was and never returned for follow up. The patient is not really concerned about the colon cancer at this time.

**Patient appearance**: The patient should be a 65-year old man or woman. The patient should appear to be in pain, and should be touching the neck and grimacing.

**Patient instructions**: The challenge for the patient is to communicate with the physician as one would naturally, without giving away too much information. If the physician uses technical terminology, ask for clarification.

**Onset**: It is hard to pinpoint exactly when it started. However, the pain seems to have developed gradually over the last several weeks.

**Location:** In the back of the neck – (point to the middle of the neck, over the bones)

**Radiation**: None.

**Quality**: Gnawing pain.

**Severity**: Several weeks ago it was a 5/10, but now it’s a 10/10.

**Course/Progression**: At first it was just an ache that would become bothersome at work. The patient sits at a desk all day. However, the pain has become increasingly worse and it is hard for the patient to get through a day’s work.

**Prior neck pain**: Nothing like this.

**Neck stiffness**: Present, and it hurts to move it.

**Duration**: Currently, it is present all day, every day.

**Factors that alleviate the pain**: The patient tried ibuprofen for the pain. It helped a bit at first, but now it does not help at all.

**Factors that exacerbate the pain:** Moving, bending it forward and back, coughing, and straining.

**Daily fluctuations**: The pain is severe at night and the patient has difficulty sleeping.

**Weakness**: The patient’s hands feel weak, as do the legs. The patient dropped a coffee mug one morning.

**Numbness:** None noted.

**Urinary dysfunction** – The patient has the sensation that his or her bladder doesn’t completely empty. There was one episode during which the patient didn’t make it to the bathroom. The patient thought he or she held it too long.

**Weight loss**: The patient has lost approximately 20 pounds over the last several months. The weight loss was unintentional.

**Fever, chills, or recent infections**: None

**Prior testing for tuberculosis**: The patient gets tested at work, and it has always been negative.

**Trauma or inciting event:** The patient doesn’t remember anything that could have triggered the pain.

**What made the patient come to the hospital now**? The pain is unbearable and it just seems to be getting worse.

**Patient’s thoughts on the cause:** The patient thought the pain might be from sitting at a desk all day or bad posture.

**Emotion**: The patient is very concerned about the pain, because it has worsened and become quite severe.

**Past medical history**: Two years ago, the patient was diagnosed with colon cancer. It was resected.

**Further details about the colon cancer:**  The patient did not follow up after the surgery. The medical bills were too expensive and the patient just wanted to get back to work.

**Medications:** The patient has tried acetaminophen, aspirin, and ibuprofen, without relief.

**Family history**: Positive for colon cancer. There is no other significant family history.

**Social history**: The patient is married, monogamous, and works in medical records.

**Alcohol** – The patient drinks only occasionally.

**Tobacco** – No history of tobacco use.

**Recreational drugs** – No history of drug use.

Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Opening Statement**: "I can't seem to get rid of this cough."

**Presentation/Affect**: You are holding a tissue and cough deeply for duration of encounter.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

**Social History:**

You are a native of Baltimore and work as an accountant for the State of Tennessee government. You have been married 28 years and have 2 children, a daughter, Amy (27), and son, David (25). David is stationed overseas in Germany and Amy lives in Nashville and has two sons, Todd (now 10) and Adam (now 7) and is currently going through a divorce. Because the divorce is not amiable, your grandsons have been staying with you for the past few months. The younger one is in the first year of grade school and the older one is in fourth grade. You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You occasionally have a glass of wine in the evenings. You have environmental allergies in the spring.

**Past Medical History:**

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. You are currently using the patch for help. Your grandson Todd has also had a sore throat last week that was diagnosed as strep throat and treated with penicillin for 7 days. His symptoms included a very sore throat and fever but no cough. He's feeling better now. If asked, "Have you ever been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)?" respond, "Not that I know of." If asked if you've had a TB test, respond, "Yes, but it has been a number of years since my last one...."

**Family History:**

* Father: had high blood pressure and smoked. Died at age 80 - 10 years ago (of old age)
* Mother: seems to be healthy but may have high cholesterol and maybe arthritis. Age 78
* Maternal grandmother: died when you were a child. Was in a nursing home and never really knew her history.
* Maternal grandfather and paternal grandparents: Died before you were born.
* Son: No known medical conditions
* Daughter: No known medical conditions

**Embedded Concern:**

As the student transitions from taking the history to begin the physical exam, say:

*"I'm really worried that I might have lung cancer."*

If asked why you think you might have lung cancer and smoking has not been disclosed say:

*"I've known some folks that had lung cancer and coughed a lot and that's why I'm worried"*

If it looks like the student will leave without offering their treatment plan (i.e. "I'm going to go check with my attending....") you need to ask (around the 2 minute warning):

*"So what do you think is going on?"*

# Headache OSCE SP instructions

Case Summary: The patient is a 22-year old woman who has had headaches in the past, but nothing like the one that started this morning. She came to the emergency department because the pain was unbearable. She is nauseated, and vomiting into an emesis basin. She is very concerned and wants to find out what is causing this.

Patient appearance: The patient should be a 20-something year-old overweight woman. If she is not overweight, she should wear a big shirt stuffed with a pillow, in order to appear obese. The patient should be well-groomed. Preferably, she should be wearing a hospital gown. However, conservative dress would also be acceptable. She is holding her head, rocking a little, and in excruciating pain. She tries to cooperate with examiner, but she is retching, holding an emesis basin (containing chicken baby food mixed with water), and shielding her eyes from the light.

Patient instructions: The challenge for the patient is to communicate with the “physician” as one would naturally, without giving away too much information. If the student uses technical terminology, ask for clarification.

Patient script:

The student will ask specific questions about the headache.

Onset: sudden onset “It just hit me.,” “One minute I was fine, the next minute I had the worst headache of my life.” It started 8 hours ago, while climbing stairs

Location: whole head and neck (feels like it hurts more one the right than on the left)

Description of pain: constant, excruciating, 10/10, throbbing, worst pain in your life. Exacerbated by vomiting, coughing, straining, and lying down. Nothing relieves pain. Neck also hurts.

Accompanying symptoms: You have sensitivity to light and sound, nausea and vomiting. No loss of vision, no double vision, not seeing flashing lights, no weakness, no numbness of extremities, no dizziness, no loss of consciousness.

Past medical history: No history of head trauma ever. You have had headaches in the past, approximately 3 times per month. The pain was localized to the temples, felt like steady pressure, and was 5/10 in intensity. You never had any of the following accompanying

symptoms: nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light or sound, no changes in vision, no weakness, no numbness of extremities, no dizziness, no loss of consciousness. Your headache today is different from your usual headaches.

Medications: You have been taking birth control pills for 2 years. You don’t remember the name of the medication. You take Tylenol occasionally for headaches, but not every day. You took some Tylenol today, when the headache started.

No known drug allergies.

Family History: Your mother has migraines. No family history of aneurysms or brain hemorrhage. No other family history.

Social History: Single. You drink 3 cups of coffee each day. You had a cup of coffee this morning, before the onset of this headache. You have not changed your caffeine intake. You cannot be pregnant, because you have not been sexually active in 3 months.

Review of systems: No history of fever or chills. No sinus congestion or upper respiratory illness.

Last menstrual period started 7 days ago.

# LGBTI Standardized Patient Case, version A (younger patient)

# CELA: Program in Human Simulation

Project: Communications Case: Ann Bonder Symptoms: n/a Patient Name: Ann Bonder Patient Complaint: Anxiety concerning risk factors for cervical cancer. Patient Presentation: Seated in chair, street clothes, concerned but not anxious Opening Statement: “My mom has cervical cancer and I’m afraid of getting it.”

Case Synopsis: The pt’s mother is currently hospitalized for complications related to treatment of advanced cervical cancer. Concerned about her own risks for cervical cancer, the pt has come to the clinic for a routine gynecologic exam and counseling about cervical cancer risk.

Standardized Patient Training Summary

You are 28 year-old Ann Bonder, daughter of Vanderbilt patient Margaret Bonder. You are an assistant casting agent at Contrast Creative in Nashville.

# Opening statement: “My mom has cervical cancer and I’m afraid of getting it”

Your mother is currently hospitalized for complications related to treatment of advanced cervical cancer. While in your mother’s room, you had a conversation with a medical student on her care team. You mentioned that you were scared that you might someday get cervical cancer. You do not want to go through what you have seen your mom experience. The student encouraged you to come to the clinic for a routine gynecologic exam and counseling about cervical cancer risk.

You do not have any specific complaints, but you are very worried about cervical cancer. Dealing with your mother’s illness has been very difficult for you; you have purposely avoided too much contact with doctors, preferring instead to let your mother make decisions for herself. You are very concerned there might be some hereditary risk that you will develop cervical cancer.

Sexual History

You are a lesbian and have been with your partner for 2 years. You are sexually active in a monogagamous relationship. You have had sex with 3 heterosexual partners, first experience at 17 in high school. In college, you began to realize you were attracted to women but tried to suppress it. You had a boyfriend in high school and dated a couple of guys for a few months in college. You had vaginal and oral sex with all of them. Condoms were used most of the time but not always. You did not have anal sex with any of them. You have no history of a sexually transmitted disease. No pelvic pain or vaginal discharge. You have never been pregnant. Your last sexual contact was 2 days ago with your partner. The two of you have vaginal and oral sex. Your last period was a week ago and you have regular periods.

You consider yourself a light smoker, smoking 3-4 cigarettes per day. You have smoked since college. You saw a nurse practitioner for the first time in college (freshman year 18) because you had painful cramps. You started your period at 13 and they last about 5 days with initial light cramping. Your last visit was “a couple of years ago”. If student specifically asks why no annual exam, you will state “just did not feel comfortable there” – perhaps an opportunity to build relationship and explore sexual orientation and lack of acceptance in system (all the questionnaire forms and provider’s advice assumed heterosexual without asking). If they probe about your discomfort, you will say “I just had a negative experience”. A third response to their continued probing might be “It it was really awkward for me because it was impersonal and the standard questionnaire interview.” You can disclose if they continue to inquire with questions that would inquire as to “what do you want them to know? Or is there anything you would want me to know”?

Since your mother’s cancer, you are now scared. You thought that the clinic here at Vanderbilt might give you a more thorough exam and help you understand your risks in light of your mother’s history. You felt very comfortable with the student you met and hoped this experience will be the same. You have heard something about a vaccine (“I saw a commercial for Guardasil on TV”) for cervical cancer and want to know if that would help.

Social History

You live with your partner Karen who you met on a set of a video shoot. If student asks who you live with, respond “my roommate”. You moved in with Karen a year ago in the house she owns in the Belmont area. She is 32 years old and has been a lesbian since 18. She had a few heterosexual partners early in high school. She has been supportive and helpful with your mother’s care. You have not shared your sexual orientation with you mom.

You have a “high deductible” insurance plan, so you must pay out of pocket first $\$ 5000$ (Your company is a small business that does not offer insurance, so you have an individual policy – your high-deductible plan helps keep premiums down). The plan comes with a health savings account that you use to cover routine visits like this. You try to avoid going to doctor and are generally healthy. You came into the clinic today just because you are so worried. The med student caring for your mom was so nice, and encouraged you to come for evaluation. Any smoking patches or other recommendations will come out of your pocket.

More details about mother:

She was diagnosed at age 47, about 3 years ago. She had skipped routine exams for about 3 years, and presented to an emergency department with heavy vaginal bleeding and a low blood count. She underwent an urgent hysterectomy and had her ovaries removed (“oophorectomy”) and some lymph nodes were removed. The tests showed cervical cancer that had spread to the lymph nodes. She was then sent to Vanderbilt for further care. She had chemo and radiation. The radiation caused all kinds of damage insider her. She started bleeding from her rectum (“proctitis”). Eventually that went away but then she started leaking urine from her vagina. They found that her bladder was damaged by the radiation and had a connection (“fistula”) to the vagina. The doctors said they couldn’t repair the leak so they had to bypass her bladder and make her urine go into a bag on her side (“urostomy”). Your dad couldn’t handle all this and left your mom 2 years ago. Your Dad really got creeped out by urostomy (urine bag); it would leak sometimes and smelled awful and he couldn’t handle the situation. The whole thing has been horrible; the bag really was the worst of all and your mom is still mad about that. Now she is in the hospital with a partial blockage of her bowels from all the scar tissue. She seems to be improving and it does not look like she will need surgery for that.

It is nice that the doctors care about how hard this has been for your family, but you really want to know what your personal risk is and what you can do to protect yourself. You do not want to go through anything like this.

Name: Ann Bonder

Past Medical History No chronic illnesses or complaints.

Family History   
Mom- Diagnosed 3 years ago with cervical cancer. Has suffered serious complications due to treatment, culminating in an urostomy.

Dad- 52 years old and in excellent health

Father left mother two years ago during her ongoing treatment. No brothers or sisters

Social History   
Light Smoker, ie- no more than 3 or 4 a day   
Alcohol – You drink wine or beer (2-3) when you go out with friends (3-4 times a month) Monogamous sexual relationship for the past two years   
Live in Belmont with your girlfriend   
You walk three times a week for exercise.   
You typically eat a healthy diet but cheat on occasion.

# Important:

1. Don’t reveal your sexual orientation unless specifically asked “what is your sexual orientation or do you have sex with men, women or both”? OR upon a good inquiry of the information underlined above.

2. If sexual orientation is not asked by student, then towards the end of the encounter you are to disclose and ask how it might affect the information regarding HPV and cervical cancer the student has shared.

“I know we didn’t talk about this but my partner is a woman. Does that change anything we’ve talked about?”

3. You should inquire about Guardiasil if the student doesn’t mention it. “I saw a commercial for Guardasil on TV- would it help?”

Patient Presentation: Seated in chair, street clothes, concerned but not anxious Opening Statement: “My mom has cervical cancer and I’m afraid of getting it.” Examinee Level: 3rd year medical student

Technical Requirements: None Additional Materials: None Case Synopsis: The pt’s mother is currently hospitalized for complications related to treatment of advanced cervical cancer. Concerned about her own risks for cervical cancer, the pt has come to the clinic for a routine gynecologic exam and counseling about cervical cancer risk.

Student instructions: Ann Bonder

You are working in the general gynecology clinic with Dr Rush. He has a new patient, Ann Bonder, who presents for a routine exam. Ann’s mother, Margaret, is currently an inpatient at Vanderbilt for complications related to treatment of cervical cancer; you are aware of the mother’s history because her case was presented by some fellow students in class. One of your classmates helping to care for the mother had a conversation with Ann in which she expressed fear that she might get cervical cancer too. Your classmate encouraged Ann to come to the clinic for an exam and counseling.

Dr. Rush also wants you to answer the patient’s questions about cervical cancer and counsel her regarding risk reduction. You will then present your discussion to him and he will accompany you to complete the exam later.
